title: Search autocomplete
tagline: Suggest the top 10 completions for every keystroke in well under 100 ms.
summary: Autocomplete is a read problem with a tight budget: the suggestions must appear before the user types the next letter, so roughly 100 ms end to end. You win by doing the work offline. Aggregate query logs into counts, precompute the top-k completions for every prefix, and serve them as a plain key lookup, cached in the browser and at the CDN. A small near-real-time path adds trending queries that the hourly build would miss.

functional: Return up to 10 completions for a prefix, ranked by popularity
Update rankings from what people actually search
Surface sudden trending queries within minutes
Never suggest blocked or offensive queries
nonfunctional: Suggestions visible within ~100 ms of a keystroke; server p99 under 20 ms
Available: if suggestions fail, search itself must still work
Stale by an hour is fine for normal queries
out_of_scope: Spelling correction and fuzzy matching (a follow-up)
Per-user personalisation beyond recent searches stored on the device

estimates.label: Origin QPS at peak
estimates.calc: 17k × 50% that miss browser and CDN caches

api.desc: Returns up to 10 strings. Cache-Control: public, max-age=300, so browsers and the CDN can reuse it.

data.name: prefix → top-k
data.store: Redis cluster or in-memory KV, sharded
data.note: Built offline and loaded as a whole new version, then swapped in. Never edited in place.

data.name: query_counts
data.note: Score = sum of daily counts × 0.9^age_in_days, so last week matters more than last year.

data.name: trending
data.note: Small and short-lived. Merged on top of the stable list at request time.

data.name: query_log
data.note: No user IDs needed for counting; drop them early.

flows.name: Keystroke, served from cache
flows.desc: Most short prefixes never reach a server.

steps.note: The user types s, y, s quickly. The client waits 150 ms after the last keystroke before sending, so a fast typist sends one request instead of three. It also keeps a small in-memory map of prefixes it has already fetched.
Send GET /suggest?q=sys. Normalise first (lower-case, trim spaces) so Sys and sys share one cache entry.
The edge keys its cache on the full URL. There are only 26 one-letter and 676 two-letter prefixes (a-z), and they are the hottest keys, so they are almost always cached.
Hit: the edge answers in ~10-20 ms from a nearby node, with no origin work at all. The browser also keeps the answer, so a backspace to sy costs nothing.
The user has typed system desi. Longer prefixes are rarer, so the CDN is less likely to have them.
Forward to any suggest replica. The service holds no state, so it scales by adding copies.
One key lookup: GET "system desi" returns the precomputed 10 completions with scores. ~1 ms. No tree walk, no sorting at request time.
In parallel, check the trending overlay for this prefix. Usually empty. If not, merge a rising query into the list by score.
Return the list with max-age=300. The CDN caches it for the next user who types the same prefix.
The browser renders the dropdown. If the response for an older prefix arrives late, discard it: only the latest request may update the UI.
The user presses Enter. Only submitted searches count as signal; half-typed prefixes are noise.
The search service appends {query, ts, locale} to a Kafka topic. Fire and forget; logging must never slow search.
Every hour a Spark job counts queries, adds them to decayed historical scores, drops queries from fewer than ~5 distinct sessions (privacy and noise), and removes blocklisted terms.

For each surviving query, emit every prefix up to 20 characters; group by prefix and keep the top 10 by score. 10M distinct queries give up to 200M (prefix, query) pairs, which collapse to ~100M distinct prefixes because short prefixes are shared.
Load the new snapshot into fresh tables, check it (row counts, spot checks), then flip a version pointer. Rollback is flipping it back.

flows.name: A trending query appears
flows.desc: Freshness the hourly build cannot give.

steps.note: The same log feeds a streaming job. It counts queries in 5-minute sliding windows and compares them with the usual rate for that hour.
A query searched 50× more than normal (a breaking news name, say) is written into the overlay for its prefixes, with a 1 h TTL.
The overlay holds a few thousand entries, not millions. By the time it expires, the hourly build has caught up and the query sits in the main table on its own merit.
The next request that misses the CDN for one of those prefixes merges the query in, capped at 2 of 10 slots. CDN copies refresh within their 5-minute TTL, so the trend shows up in minutes.

deep.title: Trie or precomputed prefix table?
deep.html:
A trie stores queries letter by letter; completing a prefix means walking to its node and then searching the subtree for the best queries. Searching the subtree on every keystroke is too slow, so real tries cache the top-k at every node. At that point the trie is just a way of computing a map from prefix to top-k list.

So store that map directly in a key-value store: one lookup per request, easy to shard, easy to replicate, rebuilt offline. The cost is memory: each query is copied into the list of every prefix it has (up to 20). With ~100M prefixes × ~320 B that is ~32 GB, which fits on a few cache nodes with replicas. Cap prefix length and drop rare queries to keep it bounded.

deep.title: Ranking and the offline build
deep.html:
• Score: decayed count, for example the sum of daily counts × 0.9^age. A query popular last year fades; one popular this week rises.
  • Map step: for query "system design" with score 900, emit ("s", ...), ("sy", ...) up to the full string.
  • Reduce step: per prefix, keep a min-heap of size 10. O(n log 10) instead of sorting everything.
  • Filters: minimum count, blocklist, and no personal data (queries that look like NRIC numbers, phone numbers or emails are dropped).

Shard the serving table by prefix. Range sharding (a-c, d-f...) is skewed because s and c are far more common than x; hash sharding spreads load evenly. Compare both in the sim.

deep.title: Caching at every layer
deep.html:
The cheapest request is the one never sent:

  1. Debounce on the client (150-300 ms) cuts requests per search from ~15 to ~5.
  2. Browser cache: a backspace returns to a prefix you already have.
  3. CDN: one-letter and two-letter prefixes are few (702 for a-z) and very hot, so the edge serves nearly all of them.
  4. Service cache: an in-process LRU of the hottest prefixes in front of the store.

Popularity is very skewed, so a small LRU absorbs most of the traffic. Try the LRU sim with a skewed key pattern. Keep TTLs short (minutes) so blocklist changes and trends show up.

deep.title: Freshness and safety
deep.html:
Hourly builds miss news that breaks at 9:05. The streaming path detects queries whose current rate is far above their usual rate and writes them to a small overlay with a TTL. Merge at request time and cap how many trending slots a list may take (say 2 of 10).

Autocomplete puts words in people's mouths, so safety matters more than for search results: a human-curated blocklist applied at build time and at request time, a minimum number of distinct users before a query is suggested, and a kill switch that purges a term from caches within minutes.

tradeoffs.choice: Compute top-k at request time or offline?
tradeoffs.why: Request time work would scan or walk many candidates per keystroke at ~8k/s. A precomputed list is one key lookup.

tradeoffs.choice: Trie in memory or KV store?
tradeoffs.why: Same answers, simpler to shard and replicate, and rebuilding means bulk-loading a new version instead of mutating a live tree.

tradeoffs.pick: No: hourly batch plus a trending overlay
tradeoffs.why: Updating ~20 prefix lists on every search costs ~20 writes per search and creates hot keys on short prefixes. A batch plus a small overlay gets freshness where it matters.
Longer TTLs save more origin load but delay trending queries and blocklist removals.

bottlenecks.issue: Short prefixes like "s" are extremely hot keys
bottlenecks.fix: They are few, so serve them from the CDN and an in-process cache on every suggest replica; the store barely sees them.

bottlenecks.issue: A bad build ships wrong or offensive suggestions
bottlenecks.fix: Validate the snapshot before the flip (row counts, blocklist re-check, diff against the last build) and keep the previous version for instant rollback.

bottlenecks.issue: Slow responses arrive out of order
bottlenecks.fix: Tag each request with a sequence number on the client and ignore any response older than the latest one shown.

followups.a: Add a fuzzy fallback: when a prefix has few or no completions, look up candidates within edit distance 1-2 (a precomputed deletion index or n-gram index) and suggest the best of those. Keep the exact prefix path as the fast default.
Merge the global list with the user's own recent searches, stored on the device. That needs no server state and keeps history private.

followups.q: How do you support several languages?
followups.a: Build one table per locale, key by (locale, prefix), and normalise per language (accents, full-width characters). For Chinese, use pinyin input as an extra prefix key.

followups.q: What if the suggest service is down?
followups.a: The search box still works; the dropdown is simply empty. The client should time out after ~300 ms and never block typing or submission.

quiz.q: Why precompute top-k per prefix instead of searching a trie on each request?
options: One key lookup per keystroke is far cheaper than walking and ranking a subtree
quiz.why: It costs memory (each query appears under every prefix) to make every request O(1).

quiz.q: What does debouncing on the client do?
options: Waits for a short pause in typing before sending, cutting request volume
quiz.why: A fast typist sends one request per pause, not one per letter.

quiz.q: A celebrity name starts trending at 9:05 and the hourly build ran at 9:00. How does it appear quickly?
options: Rebuild the whole table every minute
A streaming job writes it to a small trending overlay merged at request time
quiz.why: The overlay is small and short-lived; the next hourly build absorbs it.

quiz.q: Why hash-shard the prefix table rather than range-shard by first letter?
options: First letters are unevenly popular, so ranges create hot shards
quiz.why: Far more queries start with "s" than with "x". Hashing spreads that skew across all shards.
